The artifact ACTUALLY INTEGRATES rather than quoting - both closed forms emerge from evaluated integrals with the antiderivative formed and the limits substituted, and standard results are the OUTPUT of this procedure rather than an input to it, which was the single largest risk on this skill. Boundary: area_moment_of_inertia (signed, skill 1 of this batch) APPLIES established standard results for simple shapes about centroidal axes and explicitly cedes derivation here; the artifact carries the complement - this skill derives those results and does not take them as given. centroid_first_moments (signed) computes FIRST moments, the integral of y dA, while this skill computes the SECOND moment, the integral of y squared dA; the artifact states that the integrand differs by one power of the coordinate. parallel_axis_theorem_area (batch sibling, position 3, not yet signed) owns the TRANSFER relation between a centroidal axis and a parallel one; this skill obtains a value about whichever axis its integration LIMITS select, by direct integration only, and names position 3 as owner of the connection rather than performing it - a forward cession. composite_area_moment_of_inertia (position 4) and radius_of_gyration_area (position 5) excluded. Worked example Operator-re-derived symbolically and numerically. Case 1, rectangle of width b and height h about the CENTROIDAL x axis: horizontal strip of width b and thickness dy so dA = b dy with every point at the same y, limits from -h/2 to +h/2 because the axis passes through the centroid; I_x = b times the antiderivative y cubed over 3 evaluated between those limits = b(h cubed over 24 plus h cubed over 24) = b h cubed over 12; with b = 40 mm and h = 60 mm, I_x = 720000 mm^4. Case 2, triangle of base b along the x axis with apex at height h, about the BASE: the width is not constant, narrowing linearly from b at y = 0 to zero at y = h so the width is b(1 - y/h) and dA = b(1 - y/h) dy, limits from 0 to h; I_base = b times the integral of y squared minus y cubed over h = b times the antiderivative y cubed over 3 minus y to the fourth over 4h evaluated at h = b(h cubed over 3 minus h cubed over 4) = b h cubed over 12; with b = 90 mm and h = 60 mm, I_base = 1620000 mm^4. The artifact notes that the same closed form b h cubed over 12 arises for both cases even though shape and axis both differ, and states explicitly that the coincidence of form is not a shortcut. Distinguishing feature bites: the element construction is DECISIVE and the artifact states why the strip orientation follows from the integrand rather than asserting it; a SECOND shape whose element WIDTH VARIES with the integration variable appears, so the method cannot reduce to pulling a constant out of the integral; and the integration LIMITS are shown to determine which axis the result is about, with the rectangle taken from 0 to h instead of -h/2 to +h/2 returning 2880000 rather than 720000. HONEST LIMITATION recorded in concept, procedure and solution: checking a derived result against a tabulated standard value is available ONLY where such a value already exists FOR THAT AXIS. Case 1 cross-checks against the rectangle-about-centroidal-x result applied by area_moment_of_inertia and agrees at 720000. Case 2 has NO same-axis cross-check, because area_moment_of_inertia supplied the triangle's CENTROIDAL value of 540000 mm^4, a different axis from the base; connecting them requires the transfer relation owned by parallel_axis_theorem_area and is deliberately not performed, so for case 2 the available checks are dimensional and the element construction itself. Where no tabulated same-axis value exists the integration must stand on its own element construction and limits, which is why those steps carry the weight rather than the arithmetic. VERIFICATION PRECEDES REPORT in both arrays. Splitting element ORIENTATION at step 2, which is genuinely an axis error, from element WIDTH EXPRESSION at step 3, which is not, was the honest choice, and none of the canonical five names the act of pulling a varying factor out of an integral.
